author: Gabrielle Antonioli
bottom_line:
A passing storm will bring ~7-11 inches of new snow by Thursday. If you're traveling in areas with enough snow to keep you off the ground, there's enough snow for an avalanche. Treat all shady upper-elevation terrain and middle-elevation slopes as suspect, especially where the wind has formed drifts. Signs of instability—such as recent avalanches or a collapsing or cracking snowpack—indicate dangerous conditions. Remember that thin snow cover can also hide other hazards, such as rocks or stumps. 

We will update this General Avalanche Information product as more snow accumulates.
hazard_discussion:
Check out this recent early-season avalanche reported at the Sierra HERE. These are the sorts of avalanches we expect to see on shady slopes as access opens up and snow coverage increases. 

A storm rolling in tonight will be the biggest of the season so far. It starts as rain, and many areas could get more than 0.40 inches of rain by Tuesday night. A cold front Tuesday afternoon will turn that rain to snow, and our upper-elevation terrain should see snowfall in the double digits by Thursday.  Interestingly, many recent storm systems have favored the Galena and Eastern Mountains zone, particularly the Pioneers. So far, this area has the deepest early-season snowpack, making it the most likely place to see early-season avalanches.

What this storm is falling on matters more than how much falls. Until recently, the only surviving snow has been on shady, north-facing slopes at upper elevations, where snow from October storms has hung on through long dry spells. Last Saturday’s storm added a few more inches at higher elevations. No matter how you cut it, weeks of dry weather have left much of the surviving snow on upper-elevation slopes very weak. Thus, expect the deepest, most complex snowpack—and your best odds of triggering an avalanche— on upper-elevation slopes on the north half of the compass, especially where wind has drifted the new snow. Coverage remains thinnest in the Soldier and Wood River Valley Mountains. 

Here’s the early-season trap: snow coverage and access are slowly increasing, and slopes holding the most snow will look the most inviting. Those same slopes are where the new snow sits on the weakest base. So ignore the calendar (I know, it's already late November) and pay attention to the snow under your feet. If the snow cracks around your feet or sled, collapses with a “whumpf,” or you see fresh avalanches, back off to lower-angle terrain. Watch for drifts, pillows, and rippled surfaces that show where the wind has been loading slopes, and give those spots a wide berth.

If you get out, please send us your observations HERE. Snow depths, photos, and any signs of instability on shady slopes help us a lot this time of year.
